newsitem.title: UK: British parliament blocks Sinn Fein office plans.
newsitem.headline: British parliament blocks Sinn Fein office plans.

text.p: Two members of Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, were on Wednesday effectively barred from opening an office in Britain's parliament to which they were elected on May 1.

House of Commons Speaker Betty Boothroyd ruled that party leader Gerry Adams and chief negotiator Martin McGuinness could only use the facilities of parliament if they were prepared to be sworn in as members.

Adams and McGuinness, following traditional party policy, have refused to take the oath of allegiance to Queen Elizabeth, but had planned to maintain a parliamentary office after winning seats in Britain's general election two weeks ago.
Sinn Fein and the Irish Republican Army guerrilla organisation want to end British rule of Northern Ireland to reunite the province with the Irish republic.
"I'm not surprised," Adams told Northern Ireland radio when asked his reaction to the decision. "We gave a commitment to our electorate that we would not give a nod to an English queen."
But he said that both he and McGuinness would be going to the British parliament "to pick up our passes, look around the place and do a little press work".

Boothroyd told MPs: "Those who choose not to take their seats should not have access to the many benefits and facilities now available in this House without also taking up their responsibilities as members."
She gave Adams and McGuinness a week to change their minds.

In Sinn Fein's most successful British election campaign for decades, Adams won the constituency of West Belfast by almost 8,000 votes, while McGuinness was the victor in Mid Ulster by just under 1,900 votes.
Earlier, Sinn Fein said it would consider legal action if Adams and McGuinness were banned from using House of Commons facilities.

The IRA caused huge disruption on the British mainland during the election campaign with a series of warnings -- some genuine, some hoaxes -- of bombs being planted on major roads and at rail junctions.

It was part of the organisation's guerrilla battle to end British rule over Northern Ireland which has continued for more than 25 years, broken only by a 1-1/2 year ceasefire which ended in February 1996.
The British authorities have said Sinn Fein can only take part in all-party talks on the future of the province if the IRA implements a new, credible ceasefire.
